title: Fetch–decode–execute cycle
examples: What is the difference between a register and a memory location?
How does the CPU know what instruction to run next?
If the clock speed is high, does the CPU run faster?

explain.say: Today we learn how the computer brain works. It follows a cycle to run programs.
Registers are small storage areas inside the CPU. They hold data right now. Think of them as the CPU's quick scratchpad.
Buses are like electrical pathways connecting parts. They carry data between components. Think of them as the computer's roads.
The fetch cycle gets the next instruction from memory. The program counter tells the address. The data bus carries the instruction.
The decode cycle translates the instruction. The control unit figures out what the instruction means. It prepares the necessary components.
The execute cycle performs the action. The CPU uses the data and registers to calculate or move data. This is where the work happens.

items: Result is stored back in a register

faq.q: What is the main difference between the fetch and decode stages?
faq.a: Fetch gets the instruction from memory using an address. Decode figures out what that instruction actually means to the CPU.
asks: Does fetch just get the bits?
What happens after fetching the instruction?

faq.q: Do all instructions use the ALU?
faq.a: No, some instructions only move data or change addresses. The ALU is only needed for calculations like adding or subtracting numbers.
asks: When is the ALU not used?

faq.q: How does the CPU know which instruction to fetch next?
faq.a: The program counter register keeps track of the memory address of the next instruction. It automatically updates after each fetch.
asks: What keeps track of the next step?
Does the PC change by one every time?

faq.q: What is the role of the buses in this cycle?
faq.a: Buses act as the physical connections. They carry the address signals and the actual data between the CPU and main memory.

faq.q: Does CPU speed only depend on clock speed?
faq.a: No, performance also depends on how many registers and how fast the internal components work together.
asks: What affects processing speed besides clock speed?

facts: The Program Counter holds the memory address of the next instruction.
The Arithmetic Logic Unit performs calculations and comparisons.
The data bus transfers the actual data or instruction bits.
The cycle repeats continuously while the computer is running.

quiz.say: If the CPU needs to add two numbers, which stage is primarily responsible for the calculation?
quiz.why: The execute cycle uses the ALU to perform the required arithmetic operation.

wrong.0: This stage only retrieves the instruction, not the data for calculation.
wrong.1: This stage only interprets what the instruction means, it does no math.
wrong.2: Writing to a register is storage, not the actual calculation itself.

quiz.say: What component holds the address of the instruction to be fetched next?
quiz.why: The Program Counter is specifically designed to point to the next sequential instruction address.

wrong.0: The MAR holds the address currently being accessed, not necessarily the next one.
wrong.1: The Data Bus carries the data, it does not store the address.
wrong.2: The Control Unit manages the cycle, it does not store the next address.

quiz.say: If the data needs to move from main memory to the CPU, which bus is mainly used to carry the information?
quiz.why: The data bus is the pathway responsible for moving the actual bits of information.

wrong.0: This is too general; the Data Bus is the specific pathway for data transfer.
wrong.2: The address bus only carries the location or address, not the data itself.
wrong.3: The control bus carries timing and control signals, not the bulk data.
